presentingComplaint: Progressive redness, swelling and foul discharge from a right forefoot ulcer for 5 days, with fever, confusion and near-collapse today.
history: Type 2 diabetes for 14 years on premixed insulin, with poor glycaemic control (last HbA1c 10.2%). Known peripheral neuropathy and prior toe amputation on the left foot. Two weeks ago he noticed a painless ulcer under the right first metatarsal head after walking barefoot at a temple. Over the last 5 days the surrounding foot became red, swollen and started discharging pus with a foul odour; he continued weight-bearing. For 48h he has had high fever with rigors, reduced oral intake and today became drowsy and light-headed on standing, prompting emergency presentation. He took a course of oral cephalexin from a local pharmacy 6 days ago without improvement. No prior documented resistant organisms. Smoker, 30 pack-years.
examination: Drowsy but rousable, peripherally cool and mottled, capillary refill 4s. Right forefoot markedly swollen and erythematous extending to the mid-foot, warm and tender, with a 3 cm plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head probing to bone and discharging foul purulent material; surrounding crepitus not felt and no haemorrhagic bullae. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses not palpable bilaterally; reduced sensation to 10g monofilament. No spreading necrosis or pain out of proportion. Chest clear, abdomen soft.
imaging: Plain radiograph of the right foot: soft-tissue swelling with cortical destruction and periosteal reaction at the first metatarsal head consistent with underlying osteomyelitis; no subcutaneous gas. Bedside vascular assessment shows absent pedal Doppler signals suggesting significant peripheral arterial disease.
microbiology: Two sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics. Deep tissue/bone specimen taken at surgical debridement sent for culture. Blood cultures at 36h grew Klebsiella pneumoniae; deep tissue culture grew ESBL-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae plus meticillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus and mixed anaerobes; carbapenem-susceptible. Initial broad empiric cover (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam) de-escalated/adjusted to meropenem based on the ESBL result, with vancomycin stopped once MRSA excluded.
differentialDiagnoses: Severe (limb- and life-threatening) diabetic foot infection with osteomyelitis and septic shock
finalDiagnosis: Severe diabetic foot infection with contiguous osteomyelitis complicated by septic shock and acute kidney injury, due to ESBL Klebsiella pneumoniae with MSSA and anaerobes
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e - Soft Tissue and Diabetic Foot Infections
stewardship: Life-threatening (severe) diabetic foot infection with septic shock mandates immediate broad empiric cover after two blood cultures and a deep tissue specimen, plus early surgical debridement for source control. Empiric regimen must cover Gram-positives including MRSA (prior antibiotic exposure, severity), Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, and anaerobes: vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam. When cultures return ESBL Klebsiella with MSSA and anaerobes, de-escalate to a carbapenem (meropenem, which retains anaerobic cover) and stop vancomycin once MRSA is excluded. Duration guided by source control: 2-4 weeks for soft tissue, up to 6 weeks if residual osteomyelitis, or shorter if infected bone is fully resected. Correct hyperglycaemia and assess revascularisation given absent pulses.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast without cover) given acute kidney injury
Dose-adjust vancomycin and meropenem for renal impairment with level monitoring
Do not delay surgical debridement/source control while awaiting cultures
Avoid aminoglycoside monotherapy in the setting of AKI and PAD
edgeCases: Absent pedal pulses signal critical limb ischaemia requiring urgent vascular review; ischaemia limits antibiotic tissue penetration
If crepitus, haemorrhagic bullae or pain out of proportion develop, escalate to necrotizing fasciitis pathway with emergency exploration
Probe-to-bone positive plus raised ESR strongly predicts osteomyelitis and lengthens therapy
Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales would mandate escalation to ceftazidime-avibactam-based therapy
expectedMaiK: A severe (IDSA/IWGDF grade 4) diabetic foot infection with probe-to-bone osteomyelitis presenting in septic shock with AKI; needs blood and deep-tissue cultures, immediate broad empiric antibiotics covering MRSA/Pseudomonas/anaerobes, urgent surgical debridement for source control, and culture-directed de-escalation to a carbapenem for ESBL Klebsiella.
